query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A tailored thermo-mechanical processing route that refines the lamellar colony into an ultrafine duplex microstructure will improve both the tensile strength and room-temperature ductility of eutectic high-entropy alloys by introducing hierarchical interface constraints and microcrack-arresting boundaries.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi2.1) with coarse dual-phase lamellar colonies containing extensive internal boundaries that enable microcrack initiation under tensile deformation.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled sequence of rolling and annealing (tailored thermo-mechanical processing) to refine the microstructure into an ultrafine-grained duplex arrangement while preserving its lamellar morphology.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile deformation under standard mechanical testing conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Ultrafine grain boundaries and preserved lamellar interfaces that act as barriers to both dislocation motion and crack propagation.
generation.mechanism: The refined microstructure fosters a two-hierarchical constraint effect, where the ultrafine grains increase strength via grain-boundary strengthening and the retained lamellar interfaces serve as effective microcrack-arresting features, thereby delaying damage accumulation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified lamellar baseline, the processed alloy is expected to exhibit higher tensile strength and increased ductility, reducing the susceptibility to catastrophic room-temperature failure.
generation.baseline: The starting eutectic high-entropy alloy with conventional coarse lamellar colonies that are prone to initiating microcracks under tensile stress.
generation.boundary: The intervention’s benefits are anticipated only within an optimized range of processing parameters; excessive deformation or inappropriate annealing conditions might lead to unwanted phase transformations or coarsening that could negate these improvements.
generation.uncertainty: The exact processing parameters required to achieve the desired duplex microstructure and the quantitative improvements in mechanical properties remain to be thoroughly explored.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA specimens: one set with conventional cast and annealed lamellar microstructure (baseline) and another set subjected to the tailored thermo-mechanical processing (rolling followed by controlled annealing). Conduct standard room-temperature tensile tests and perform microstructural characterization using high-resolution electron microscopy.
measurements: Observation of microcrack propagation and arrest at interfaces
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the processed samples do not demonstrate a statistically significant increase in both tensile strength and ductility compared to the baseline, or if microscopic analysis fails to reveal the anticipated ultrafine duplex microstructure with effective microcrack-arresting boundaries, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Enhanced strength–ductility synergy in ultrafine-grained eutectic high-entropy alloys by inheriting microstructural lamellae

Abstract: Realizing improved strength–ductility synergy in eutectic alloys acting as in situ composite materials remains a challenge in conventional eutectic systems, which is why eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs), a newly-emerging multi-principal-element eutectic category, may offer wider in situ composite possibilities. Here, we use an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA to engineer an ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure that deliberately inherits its composite lamellar nature by tailored thermo-mechanical processing to achieve property combinations which are not accessible to previously-reported reinforcement methodologies. The as-prepared samples exhibit hierarchically-structural heterogeneity due to phase decomposition, and the improved mechanical response during deformation is attributed to both a two-hierarchical constraint effect and a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism.
